rationale: Amundi's own chief operating officer, Guillaume Lesage, states that “All our employees have access to our ALTO Studio platform and half of them use it on a weekly basis” and that “We already have 20 real applications to asset management” — of which the single named example is compliance software “which allows a marketer to check that their proposal is compliant” (company claims: both statements are first-party and no independent T1/T2 source corroborates them at that magnitude). One named tool is independently dated and corroborated: Amundi's Compliance Assistance tool, built on ALTO Studio to “analyze the compliance of a document against a defined set of rules, and the consistency of its content”, won “The Most Promising Project Using Gen AI” at the AM Tech Day Awards on 8 October 2024, and WatersTechnology reported in March 2025 that Alto Studio — which it describes as Amundi's “internal data platform” — “has 500 users at the buy-side firm” among “teams of researchers, quants, and financial analysts”. A named production tool plus a firm-wide internal GenAI environment with an independently reported internal user count clears the piloting bar. Stops short of scaling: the only disclosed penetration figure is weekly rather than daily use by about half of staff, exactly one of the claimed 20 applications is named in any fetched source, the agentic layer is described by Lesage as “the latest development to come”, which METHODOLOGY §4 counts as intent rather than deployment, and no fetched T1/T2 source names AI a formal strategic priority — Amundi's February 2026 full-year results release does not mention AI at all.
footnote: Scope and sourcing calls. Excluded under METHODOLOGY §1(a): Amundi Technology's ALTO platform (ALTO Investment, ALTO Wealth & Distribution, ALTO Asset Servicing) and the AI engines Lesage says Amundi plans to offer to ALTO clients from the second half of 2025 are software Amundi sells to third-party managers, banks and wealth platforms — only statements about Amundi's own staff using ALTO Studio were counted toward the stage. The AM Tech Day award page does not itself disambiguate whether the Compliance Assistance tool is internal or a client module; the internal attribution rests on WatersTechnology calling Alto Studio Amundi's “internal data platform” with 500 users at the firm, and on Lesage's marketer example. Excluded under §1(b): Amundi Investment Institute research about AI as a market theme and AI-thematic funds such as CPR Invest — Artificial Intelligence. No source was found stating that Crédit Agricole group AI programmes cover Amundi's own staff or operations, so none were counted. name: Citadel
rationale: Citadel LLC — the multi-strategy hedge fund, distinct from the separately run market maker Citadel Securities — has at least two named AI systems in production for investment staff. The internally built Citadel AI Assistant, a chatbot trained on licensed data including transcripts, regulatory filings, brokerage research and the firm's own strategies, was reported in December 2025 to surface risks, generate tailored research and create reading lists aligned to an investor's portfolio, and to see regular use across almost all of the firm's equities investors (company claim, via CTO Umesh Subramanian); by May 2026 Head of Core Engineering Atte Lahtiranta described analysts using Claude for Excel to build and update coverage models, separate signal from noise and pressure-test their work (company claim). Both disclosures explicitly retain human authority — Subramanian cautioned that investment decisions remain for humans — which is precisely the augmentation constraint that defines scaling. Stops short of embedded: no public evidence of investment decisions taken without a human in the loop and no disclosed redesign of the organisation around AI; confidence is held at med rather than high because the single penetration figure is a company claim scoped to equities investors rather than the whole multi-strategy firm, and citadel.com returned 403 on every page tried, so no first-tier own-domain corroboration could be read.
footnote: Scope and sourcing calls. Citadel Securities, the electronic market maker, is a separate firm and none of its material was counted here; note that the Anthropic page names only "Citadel" without disambiguating the two, so that event is attributed to the hedge fund on the strength of the speaker's role and the investment-research content of the quote (coverage models, separating signal from noise), while the Hedgeweek event is unambiguous (equities investors, portfolio managers). Excluded under METHODOLOGY §1(b): Citadel's 2026 acquisition of the bulk of the equity book of the AI-focused fund Situational Awareness is an investment position, not operational adoption. Also excluded on tier: an eFinancialCareers interview with Umesh Subramanian describing portfolio managers interacting with Citadel's AI tools via chatbot and roughly a decade of machine-learning use, which is third-tier and corroborates only. Pre-2023 quantitative and machine-learning history informs context but is not an event here.

name: Two Sigma

By January 2026 CTO Jeff Wecker wrote that "everyone at Two Sigma is expected to use LLMs to accelerate their work," and the head of its Complex Feature Engines team said AI "has turbocharged this ability for us, creating sets of insights that would have taken months to create in just days." The organisation was built to match: a dedicated AI and machine learning team was created in May 2024 to define and implement firm-wide AI/ML strategy, and its leader was promoted that August to Chief Investment Officer of Two Sigma Investments, credited on the firm's own site with fuelling "significant growth in the company's machine learning and AI alpha generation." Stops short of embedded: every sourced description keeps human scientists framing the question and verifying the output, with no public evidence of decisions taken without a human in the loop or of the firm being restructured around AI; confidence is held at med rather than high because the deployment claims are self-published on twosigma.com with no disclosed penetration metric, and the independent trade coverage of the AI leadership build-out traces back to a single Bloomberg report.

name: CSOP Asset Management
rationale: CSOP runs multiple AI use cases in daily production across separate functions, documented in two Microsoft releases sixteen months apart. By May 2024 a bespoke Azure OpenAI chatbot and an email pre-classification system were live for sales, senior management, HR and the operations middle office, credited with boosting information-retrieval efficiency by 20% and filtering out 80% of non-essential correspondence (company claims), with the Azure build having started in October 2023. By September 2025 CSOP had stood up an “Intelligence Hub” on Azure AI Foundry and GitHub Copilot that lets departments build their own applications without coding, carrying three named production tools: an automated ETF reporting portal in Operations (10 minutes down to 30 seconds), trade-data extraction from multi-format confirmations in Trading (60+ minutes down to near-instant), and an analytics tool built by Deputy CEO and Chief Investment Officer Yi Wang that reads stock charts and sell-side research to generate trading ideas for internal reference, with Wang describing one to two hours a day of manual extraction reclaimed. Governance is a deployment gate rather than a published policy — solutions undergo IT review “to ensure security, compliance, and alignment with core AI principles.” Stops short of embedded: the investment tool feeds ideas “for internal reference” with humans making the call, and no public source shows autonomous decisions or an organisation redesigned around AI. Confidence is held at med rather than high because every fact rests on Microsoft-authored vendor pages — headline figures such as a “30x leap in efficiency, 99% automation in key workflows” are unverifiable vendor and company claims, no independent trade-press corroboration was locatable, and csopasset.com returned 403, so no own-domain confirmation could be read.
footnote: Scope and sourcing calls. Everything counted here is internal-facing: Microsoft's September 2025 story places the Intelligence Hub and its applications inside CSOP's own Operations, Trading and Investment teams with no indication they are offered to clients, so METHODOLOGY §1(a) does not bite; enterprise-productivity uses (knowledge chatbot, email triage, HR candidate shortlisting, GitHub Copilot for internal development) are counted because §1 covers operations the firm runs for itself. Tier note: both events rest on Microsoft's own domains, which are first-tier for the engagement they announce, but they are one vendor's voice — two separate releases sixteen months apart rather than two independent observers — which is why confidence is med and not high. AUM is CSOP's own “About CSOP” boilerplate in its 30 July 2026 PRNewswire release, as at 30 June 2026 (about US$45.3 billion / HK$355.0 billion). csopasset.com/en/about/overview returned 403, so no first-party website corroboration of either the AI deployments or the AUM could be read.

name: State Street Investment Management (SSGA)
rationale: State Street's asset-management arm puts AI inside the investment process itself: a January 2026 piece by Global Head of Research Alexander Rudin and Head of Data and Analytics Minkyu Kim states that “machine learning (ML) and AI have become integral to our investment process, supporting use cases from trading to forecasting”, that “We have made an AI-powered chatbot available to our investment teams” whose researchers “use it extensively as a research assistant”, and that the Systematic Equity team “employs a suite of factors based on NLP” — including neural-network embeddings — over earnings-call transcripts and regulatory filings (company claims; no penetration or daily-use figure is disclosed). The enterprise scaffolding behind it is disclosed on State Street Corporation's own earnings calls: CFO John Woods said in April 2026 that the firm has “built a centralized AI hub, which has a very deep use case pipeline” and that “This platform supports over 200 AI use cases now, with 70 of those already live”, with “Virtually every employee, where it makes sense” holding access and “all of our developers” on AI-assisted development tools, and said in July 2026 that State Street had “delivered agentic capabilities from a standardized copilot platform to all eligible employees”. Stops short of embedded: the firm's own framing is that “AI is not replacing our human judgement—it's amplifying it”, it says of generative AI that “we're not yet comfortable using it for direct investment modeling”, and its most concretely described new model — an XGBoost forecaster of company fundamentals — “has not been implemented in live portfolios”. Confidence is held at med rather than high because the investment-process evidence, the part that distinguishes this asset manager from its custody-bank parent, rests on a single first-party article with no independent corroboration and no disclosed adoption metric, while the 70-live-use-case count and the copilot rollout are reported at corporation level and never broken out by division.
footnote: Scope and sourcing calls. Excluded under METHODOLOGY §1(a): the AI State Street sells to clients through the Alpha platform and its AI-enhanced Alpha Data Platform — a product line, not internal adoption. Also not counted: the custody and fund-servicing AI described on State Street's Alpha insights page (ML predictive NAV benchmark, predictive reconciliation matching and break resolution, anomaly detection on vendor market data, document digitisation) — that page carries no visible publication date, so it can support only that the work exists and not a dated event, and it is servicing State Street performs for clients rather than its own investment operations. Entity scope: this row is the asset manager (State Street Investment Management, formerly State Street Global Advisors); the centralized AI hub, the 70 live use cases and the standardized copilot platform are disclosed at State Street Corporation level and cover all eligible employees, Investment Management included, but are never broken out by division — recorded here as firm-wide rather than attributed to the investment arm. Forward-looking figures on the same calls (a 30–40% expected developer-productivity gain, tangible business impact expected in H2 2026, $1B transformation benefits by 2029) are intent under §4 and do not carry the stage. AUM is the $6.28 trillion State Street Investment Management reports on its own “Who we are” page as at 30 June 2026. Unusable: State Street Corporation's FY2025 Form ARS on sec.gov and a FinAI News piece on the 2026 AI roadmap both returned 403 to every attempt.

footnote: Scope and sourcing calls. Chief Investment Officer reported on 2023-10-31 that Saifr — the natural-language tool Fidelity Labs introduced the year before — is used by Fidelity's portfolio managers, sales and other staff to flag brand, reputational and regulatory risk in communications they are drafting, in real time while emails, presentations and speeches are being created, and that Fidelity also runs materials for funds it is launching through it. AWS's write-up of its re:Invent 2025 conference records a second, unrelated internal system: an enterprise-scale text-to-SQL solution, reported at 93–95% execution accuracy and about 28-second response times, that lets non-technical staff query complex internal databases in natural language. Stops short of scaling: neither source shows daily firm-wide production or names AI a strategic priority backed by deployment evidence — the AWS item describes a capability Fidelity "showcased" at a conference rather than one it states is in production, the Chief Investment Officer piece is framed around what staff "can" do with the tool and discloses no user count, deployment date or penetration figure, no fetchable T1/T2 source puts AI inside the investment process itself, and the piloting bar's governance leg (an AI use policy or committee) has no fetchable T1/T2 source either — so the row rests on two shipped but contained use cases, which clears exploring and stops there.

name: Permodalan Nasional Berhad (PNB)

name: J.P. Morgan Asset Management
rationale: J.P. Morgan Asset Management has moved named generative-AI tools into its own investment workflow, and one of them is now in full production: in January 2026 the firm cut ties with proxy advisers ISS and Glass Lewis and will "rely solely on an internal, AI-driven voting platform called Proxy IQ" for US shareholder voting, described as "the first such move by a major asset manager", with IPE reporting a month later that the tool "will handle the data collection, research and recommendations that its proxy advisers previously handled". The two AI tools documented inside the investment process itself are still described by JPMAM's own executives as pilots: SpectrumGPT, a GPT-4 tool running in JPMorgan's cloud that drafts research notes from unstructured data, was "still being tested and evaluated" with fundamental equity portfolio managers in October 2023, and "Moneyball", which shows portfolio managers how they and the market behaved in comparable past situations to correct for behavioural bias, was "a pilot program still being developed" in June 2024. Human authority is explicit in both strands — global head of data science Arezu Moghadam on SpectrumGPT: "I'm still the decision maker here, I'm still the accountable person here" — and the firm says Proxy IQ will "extend the high bar of independent analysis that our portfolio managers, research analysts and stewardship teams have always applied to every vote" (company claim). Stops short of scaling: no source read shows SpectrumGPT or Moneyball reaching production, no penetration or daily-use figure is disclosed for any of the three tools, no AM-specific AI use policy or governance committee surfaced, and the only current-tense claim that AI runs across the investment platform sits on an undated own-domain page that can support existence but cannot date a deployment — so between piloting and scaling, METHODOLOGY §4 picks the lower.
footnote: Scope and sourcing calls. Parent-bank split, the central call on this row: JPMorgan Chase's firm-wide "LLM Suite" assistant had reached roughly 50,000 of the bank's 240,000 global employees by July 2024, with an internal email telling the Asset & Wealth Management division it would be next to receive access — that is BANK-WIDE evidence and is NOT counted here. This row rests only on sources specifically about the asset manager's own investment process, following the same bank-vs-asset-management split that produced this project's Goldman Sachs Asset Management defer. Excluded under §1(a): the "Whole Portfolio Distribution solution" delivered to clients through FactSet and powered by J.P. Morgan's Fusion (WatersTechnology, 2026-05-01, read in full) is a product sold to clients, not internal adoption. Excluded under §1(b): am.jpmorgan.com's Artificial Intelligence market-themes page is entirely AI-as-investment-opportunity content written for clients. Sourcing: JPMAM's own Spectrum page calls Spectrum "how we invest" and SpectrumIQ "our suite of AI capabilities", but carries only an "as of December 2025" data stamp rather than a visible publication date, so it supports existence and is deliberately not cited as an event. AUM is J.P. Morgan Asset Management alone — "$4 trillion (as of 9/30/2025)" from the firm's own press-release boilerplate — deliberately NOT the "more than $7 trillion in client assets" Asset & Wealth Management figure quoted in the January 2026 proxy coverage. Tooling walls hit: pionline.com and cnbc.com both returned 403, and the 2025 JPMorgan Chase Investor Day Asset & Wealth Management deck fetched as an image-only PDF with no text layer — a human should retry that deck, as Investor Day materials are the likeliest carrier of AM-specific adoption metrics.

name: TPG Inc.
rationale: TPG runs internally built, customized LLM tools across the whole firm: CEO Jon Winkelried told the Q1 2026 earnings call that engineers inside TPG's own tech group have built tools “rolled out systematically to the firm” on top of large language models, and that “probably something approaching 80% of the firm now is using — are using these tools on an active daily basis” (company claim — the penetration figure is first-party and could not be corroborated externally). A second internal system is already shipped: Lab 39, TPG's in-house AI team since 2019, built “Samantha, which is our agentic platform or orchestrator,” used to interrogate the firm's own research and diligence data. Decision authority stays human by TPG's own account — “Ultimately, the investment decision remains with the humans in the room, but it's a very powerful supplement to the discussion” — which is the defining scaling constraint. Stops short of embedded: TPG claims no autonomous decisions and no org redesign around AI, and the one tool pointed at the investment decision itself — a purpose-built TPG AI assistant that would give the investment committee a weekly risk/opportunity report — is described in future tense (“a tool that will ingest documents and data every week”), which METHODOLOGY §4 reads as intent and does not count toward the stage.
footnote: Scope and sourcing calls. Counted under §1 as operations TPG runs for itself: the firm-wide LLM productivity tooling and the Samantha research/diligence orchestrator. Excluded under §1(a)/(b): the “more than $4 billion of initial capital” TPG committed on its Q2 2026 call “to form a new AI transformation and services platform” (DeployCo, with OpenAI) — capital placed into an AI venture that sells deployment services to others, not TPG's own operating model — and TPG's AI-as-thematic-investing. Excluded under §1(c): portfolio-company AI value creation, which TPG itself calls “applied AI, where we bring the science to our companies,” plus its systematic AI-disruption risk review of the portfolio and portfolio software bookings attributed to AI. Not counted under §4: the investment-committee AI assistant, stated in future tense. Sourcing limit: both load-bearing sources are TPG's own — a December 2025 issue of its Flywheel newsletter and its own official earnings call — and no independent outlet could be read to corroborate the 80% figure or Samantha (Bloomberg's 2026-02-18 report on a TPG AI taskforce returned HTTP 403; Private Equity International's 2026-05-01 interview is registration-gated), which is why confidence is med rather than high. AUM is total AUM as at 2026-06-30.

name: Manulife Investment Management
aliases: Manulife Global Wealth and Asset Management
rationale: Manulife has evidence consistent with Scaling. Its public-markets investment teams use the proprietary AI Research Assistant in daily research workflows; more than two-thirds of public-markets investment personnel were using AI as of August 31, 2025, and the tool accelerates synthesis of financials, transcripts, internal notes, news and commentary while keeping investment decisions with humans.   By May 2026, Manulife Wealth & Asset Management had additionally put three AI-powered tools into production across Canada Wealth, U.S. Retirement and U.S. Retail, covering compliance Q&A, advisor-outreach intelligence and sales/meeting intelligence; the company reports nearly 980 users and 5,400+ conversations for the Canadian tool, nearly 2,000 opportunities and ~390 closed deals for the retirement tool, and a ~40% increase in contact rate for the retail tool.   Manulife explicitly describes these as part of its strategic priority of becoming an “AI-powered organization,” and says its AI strategy spans research and distribution with governance and human oversight.     At the parent level, more than 70% of Manulife’s global workforce is engaged with GenAI tools, including ChatMFC.
footnote: Scope and entity calls. The September and October 2025 releases establish the AI Research Assistant as a live internal investment-process tool within Manulife Wealth & Asset Management’s public-markets teams, with 65% adoption shortly after launch and more than two-thirds of public-markets investment personnel using AI by August 2025. The May 2026 update adds three further internal production deployments across Wealth, U.S. Retirement and U.S. Retail, including a compliance-policy Q&A assistant, advisor-outreach tool and sales platform, with reported usage and outcome metrics. These are counted as internal operational adoption because they are employee-facing tools used within Manulife WAM businesses rather than AI products sold to clients. The parent-level claim that more than 70% of Manulife’s global workforce engages with GenAI, including ChatMFC, is retained as supporting enterprise evidence but is not used to establish investment-team penetration. All cited adoption and impact figures are company-reported; no independent corroboration is established in the source set.

name: AP Pension
rationale: AP Pension's public AI record from 2023 onward is intent and enablement, not deployment. Its enterprise data foundation is live on Microsoft Fabric — Head of Data Platform Jacob Rønnow Jensen walks through the build in Microsoft's own dated customer story (2024-05-23) — but that same story puts AI itself in the future, saying the organisation "is keen to explore additional out-of-the-box capabilities like data quality, data catalog, and Copilots and AI to enhance its services and operational efficiency". A year later AP Pension's own newsroom announced a new Festina Finance core system live from 1 May 2025, with CIO Pia Werner Alexandersen saying it "muliggør mere innovative produkter, automatiserede processer ved hjælp af AI" ("enables more innovative products, automated processes through AI") and calling it "et vigtigt skridt mod at modernisere vores digitale platforme ved at anvende AI" ("an important step toward modernising our digital platforms by applying AI") — a platform described as making AI possible, not an AI use case that has shipped; the chairman/CEO letter in Årsrapport 2025 (p. 4) repeats that phrasing nearly verbatim. The annual report (published March 2026, approved 16 Apr 2026) is the firm's most direct statement and the closest it comes to piloting: p. 6 says "vi øger brugen af AI til at effektivisere kundeoplevelsen" ("we are increasing the use of AI to make the customer experience more efficient") and that it "gennemfører ... et større udrulnings- og træningsforløb" ("is carrying out a larger rollout and training programme") for colleagues — present tense, but the rollout is unnamed, the AI is unnamed, the same page frames data quality as a "forudsætning for en optimal fremtidig udnyttelse af AI" ("prerequisite for optimal future exploitation of AI"), and p. 23 still "stræber efter at bruge AI-teknologier" ("strives to use AI technologies"). Governance is dated but not AI-specific: a non-statutory board Teknologiudvalg (Technology Committee) met 7 times in 2025 with "kunstig intelligens" among nine listed topics alongside cloud, outsourcing and data protection (p. 22), and a Dataetisk Forum reports to it (p. 23); no AI policy is named. Stops short of piloting: no public source from 2023 onward names an AI system in production at AP Pension or discloses a pilot in a named team, and the firm's 2026 annual-results release makes no AI claim at all while putting "anvendelsen af data og automatisering" among the year ahead's priorities — future tense, which METHODOLOGY §4 reads as intent. Confidence is med rather than high because the p. 6 present-tense language is the strongest adoption-adjacent claim on record and would flip the call the moment a named system or team surfaces, and one document that could settle the call remains unreadable to this toolchain (see footnote).
footnote: Two documents were flagged as unreadable to the automated toolchain. (1) Årsrapport 2025, AP Pension livsforsikringsaktieselskab (CVR 18530899; 66 pp., Danish; PDF dated 2026-03-04; approved at AGM 2026-04-16) has since been read via manual upload. AI-relevant content: p. 4 chairman/CEO letter (core system enables automated processes "ved hjælp af blandt andet AI"); p. 6 strategy section (Fabric as foundation, data quality as prerequisite for future AI, Cognizant partnership for process automation during dual-system migration, subsection "AI og data er grundlæggende for fremtidig succes" containing the rollout/training and "øger brugen af AI" claims); p. 9–10 market commentary (AI as an equity theme and valuation risk — investment view, not adoption); p. 22 governance (Teknologiudvalget: Flemming Windfeld chair, Jesper Munck Loiborg, Birgitte Birn Køngerskov; 7 meetings 2025; AI in scope); p. 22–23 data-ethics statement (nine principles incl. "ansvarlig brug af teknologi"; Dataetisk Forum). Absent anywhere in the report: a named AI system, tool, vendor, pilot team, metric, AI policy, or EU AI Act reference; nothing on AI in the investment function. Page refs are printed "Side" numbers (PDF page = printed + 1).

name: Colonial First State
rationale: CFS has a broad, measured internal generative-AI deployment: it began with "300 Copilot licences in January 2024" and by July 2024 Microsoft's own account reports "75 per cent of employees now have access to the generative AI tool", with "all of our pilot proramme users believe that Copilot is saving them time" and "40 per cent saving more than 30 minutes per day" (company claim — every penetration and productivity figure is CFS self-reported through Microsoft's newsroom, with no independent measurement). A five-year agreement with Microsoft signed 30 July 2024 and announced on CFS's own newsroom names cloud and generative AI as a strategic commitment and itemises the Azure OpenAI Service work: a service "trained on our extensive library of documents on superannuation legislation" for the FirstTech technical advisory team, member-feedback analysis, and contact-centre agent assistance. Stops short of scaling: only the enterprise assistant is evidenced as broadly used, the FirstTech legislation service is confined to a single team, and the remaining Azure OpenAI use cases are framed as "working on" and "exploring" — future tense, which METHODOLOGY §4 reads as intent one stage below where it points — while no public source places AI anywhere inside CFS's own investment process, and neither T1 source discloses an AI policy or governance committee, so the piloting call rests on deployment breadth rather than the governance leg of the bar.
footnote: Scope and sourcing calls. Enterprise-productivity, technical-advisory and contact-centre uses are counted under METHODOLOGY §1 as operations CFS runs for itself; none is an AI product sold to clients (§1a), an investment thesis (§1b) or a portfolio-company programme (§1c). The FirstTech superannuation-legislation service is counted on the basis that it assists CFS's own technical staff, even though those staff in turn support external financial advisers — a borderline §1(a) call flagged here for the reviewer. Three signals were seen and NOT counted. (1) CFS's 2026 appointment of a Group Executive for AI and Data / Chief AI Officer (Sid Baidwan, joined June 2026) overseeing an AI Centre of Excellence plus AI strategy, governance, platforms and architecture — the only carriers found are an executive-search firm's announcement, iTnews and LinkedIn, all T3, and CFS's own About Us page does not list the role, so nothing can date the event; this is the single highest-value human retry on this row, because it would supply both a 2026 event and the missing governance evidence. (2) "Australians open to AI, but still want people in charge" (CFS media release, 2026-03-11) is consumer survey research, not internal adoption. (3) CFS is 55% owned by an affiliate of KKR and 45% by Commonwealth Bank of Australia; CBA's own AI programme belongs to a separate institution and is excluded under the arm/sibling rule. Sourcing limit: both events trace to the same July-2024 Microsoft/CFS announcement cycle and one publisher lineage, and no qualifying T1/T2 source dated after 2024 was found, so confidence is med rather than high. AUM is the "A$150 billion assets under management" stated in Microsoft's 2024-07-24 feature; CFS's own About Us page gives only a narrower, undated entity-level figure ("AIL manages more than $110.7 billion").

name: Liontrust Asset Management
rationale: Liontrust's own annual financial report announcement (24 June 2026) states that "[o]ver the past year, we have scaled the use of AI across Liontrust as a key focus of our Technology, Data and Digital objective" and that "AI is now embedded in a range of investment, operational and client reporting processes, improving efficiency and insight generation", enabled by investment in its data platform and "supported by a formal governance framework, ensuring that adoption is controlled, transparent and aligned with our regulatory status" (company claim — the entire deployment account is one paragraph of the Chair's statement). That governance framework plus real, if unquantified, usage clears the piloting bar, and the firm's own filings show the movement: seven months earlier the half-year report (20 November 2025) described teams merely reviewing "how they can enhance the execution of their processes, including through the appropriate application of AI". Stops short of scaling: no AI use case, tool or system is named anywhere in the public record, no penetration, headcount or daily-use figure is disclosed, and no independent source corroborates the claim, so the asserted "range of processes" cannot be tested against the scaling bar's requirement for deployment evidence rather than assertion — and where the evidence genuinely supports either of two adjacent stages, METHODOLOGY §4 takes the lower.
footnote: Scope and sourcing calls. Client-reporting AI is counted: it is back-office work Liontrust runs for itself, not an AI product sold to clients (§1a). Excluded under §1(b): the Liontrust Global Technology Fund's AI-themed positioning and its managers' commentary on AI reshaping market leadership — portfolio views, not internal adoption. One signal was seen but NOT counted: a BusinessWire release dated 9 April 2025 announcing that Boosted.ai had partnered with the Liontrust Global Equities team to build proprietary AI research agents, quoting team head Mark Hawtin. It would be the row's only named, team-level tool and its strongest piloting evidence, but businesswire.com timed out on three separate fetch attempts and boosted.ai returned HTTP 402, so under the public-source rule the claim is unusable here — this is the row's top human browser retry. Sourcing limit: both cited sources are Liontrust's own successive Chair's statements, i.e. one voice across two filings rather than two independent voices, which caps confidence at med. AuMA is £21,445m as at 19 June 2026; the 31 March 2026 financial-year-end figure is £19,554m.

name: Azimut Holding
rationale: Azimut Holding's public AI record from 2023 onward contains one named AI system in production, which is enough for piloting and no more. On 14 Oct 2024 Azimut Holding S.p.A. (AZM.IM) announced the launch of "Goal Based Plan", described in the release's own subhead as "un nuovo servizio che potenzia il processo di consulenza finanziaria con il supporto dell'Intelligenza Artificiale" ("a new service that strengthens the financial advisory process with the support of Artificial Intelligence"). The platform is vendor-built — "frutto della collaborazione con Wealthype, azienda italiana specializzata in intelligenza artificiale (IA) e data analytics per il settore del wealth management di cui il Gruppo Azimut possiede una partecipazione" ("the result of collaboration with Wealthype, an Italian company specialising in AI and data analytics for wealth management in which the Azimut Group holds a stake") — and the AI's role is specific: it processes advisor-held client data to map the client's "DNA finanziario" across age, profession, income prospects, wealth, risk tolerance and ESG appetite, scores the relevance of 10 predefined goals in three categories, and feeds a Financial Wellness Index from 0 to 100 that is monitored over time and reported to clients quarterly. The advisor stays in the loop by design: "Una volta suggerito il grado di rilevanza di ciascun obiettivo da parte della piattaforma IA, il consulente integra la proposta intervenendo in base alla conoscenza diretta del cliente" ("Once the AI platform has suggested the relevance of each goal, the advisor integrates the proposal based on direct knowledge of the client"). Wealthype CEO Serena Torielli names a second AI-enabled feature in the same release, "il Modulo di Ingaggio per i clienti prospect" ("the Engagement Module for prospect clients"), and says advisors were involved throughout the build. This clears the piloting bar because the source names the system, dates its launch, identifies the deploying entity (Azimut Capital Management SGR's Italian advisor network) and describes a live, recurring client output rather than a capability the platform makes possible. Stops short of scaling: the release is launch-day, so no source discloses how many advisors or clients are on the platform, no post-launch source confirms continued operation or expansion, the capability sits in a partner's platform rather than in-house, and both use cases are on the distribution and advisory side — nothing public places AI in Azimut's portfolio-management, risk, or operations functions, and no AI policy or governance body is dated. Confidence is med rather than high because the production claim rests on a single company source with no independent corroboration and no adoption metrics, and med rather than low because that source is a primary, dated, on-point disclosure rather than enabling language
footnote: Scope and sourcing calls. Counted as internal: Goal Based Plan is used by Azimut's own exclusive adviser network to build client allocations — Azimut's own portfolio-construction workflow — and is not licensed or sold to outside advisers or institutions, so it is not a §1(a) client product. It does sit close to that line, because the output reaches the client through the adviser, and a reviewer could reasonably read it the other way. Wealthype is a separate AI and data-analytics company in which Azimut Group holds a stake; the evidence used here is about Azimut's advisers running the platform, not about Azimut improving Wealthype's own operations, so it is not a §1(c) portfolio-company story — the stake is flagged for transparency. Excluded under §1(b) without being counted or cited: Azimut's AI-sector venture and co-investment activity, which surfaced at search level and was deliberately not fetched because it cannot move the stage either way. Sourcing limits: both AI events rest on Milano Finanza, staff-bylined (Hillary di Lernia, 11 January 2024; Marco Capponi, 15 October 2024) and confirmed not to be executive op-eds; Azimut's own press release on the Goal Based Plan launch returned HTTP 403, azimut.it/azimut-intelligence rendered no AI content to the fetcher, and azimut-group.com/media returned no pre-2026 releases, so no T1 corroboration was obtainable. Top human browser retries: the Azimut Goal Based Plan press release PDF on euroborsa.it, and a 2026 Hubbis interview on Azimut and "agentic AI" that returned HTTP 403 on three attempts and could move the stage if it is staff-written and confirms production agentic workflows. Name-collision warning for the monitor: Azimut-Benetti, the unrelated luxury-yacht builder, also announces onboard AI and dominates searches for "Azimut Intelligence". AuM is €157.8bn as at end-July 2026.

name: Ilmarinen
rationale: Ilmarinen's entire public AI record is governance and strategy, launched in a single two-week burst in February 2024 and maintained since as a governance artifact without advancing into disclosed deployment. On 2024-02-29 the firm published five principles for responsible AI use — humans lead AI, transparency and explainability, equal customer service, good governance, and trustworthy and secure AI systems — and named Maija Nikula as "Ilmarisen yritysarkkitehtuurista, tietoturvasta ja tekoälykehittämisestä vastaava johtaja" (director responsible for Ilmarinen's enterprise architecture, information security and AI development), under the framing quote "Teknologian ei saa antaa viedä mennessään, ihminen pitää aina ohjaksista kiinni" ("technology must not be allowed to run away with things; a human must always hold the reins"). Seventeen days earlier, technology and development director Mikko Lantto had published the strategy piece "Teknologiaosasto ei synnytä tekoälykästä yritystä" ("a technology department does not create an AI-capable company"), which argues that organisational readiness rather than the technology function determines whether AI is adopted, and names no tool, team, or deployment. The principles document itself ("Tekoälyn käytön vastuullisuusperiaatteet", 4 pp., undated) shows the governance layer is live: the board approves and re-evaluates the principles at least annually, the CEO is authorised to issue more detailed internal guidance reported to the board annually within Compliance reporting, and the text names Regulation (EU) 2024/1689 as its key applicable regulation — a number that did not exist until Official Journal publication on 12 July 2024, so the current version post-dates the February launch. Its present-tense commitments to map impacts "ennen niiden käyttöönottoa" ("before their deployment") and to monitor "tekoälyjärjestelmiemme" ("our AI systems") actively and regularly are policy language, not disclosure: no system, team, process or user count is named anywhere. Its own site describes the firm as 「使用 AI 进行投资的对冲基金」 (a hedge fund that uses AI to invest) and states 「2016 年 10 月 21 日第一份由深度学习生成的交易仓位上线执行」 and 「2017 年全面应用深度学习技术进行交易」 — first deep-learning-generated trading position live on 21 October 2016, deep learning applied across trading from 2017 (company claims, on own-domain pages that carry no visible date); 21世纪经济报道 (14 January 2026, 记者陈归辞) restates both dates as fact and puts 「管理规模已超700亿元」 (AUM above RMB 70bn) and a 2025 mean return of 56.55% behind them, which is a production use case putting live investment decisions and material capital behind the models. The supporting AI stack is first-party and dated: on 27 June 2023 幻方-基础研究 published HAI-LLM, an in-house large-model training framework 「基于萤火集群的特性而自研」 (custom-developed for the firm's own 萤火 GPU cluster) that implements four parallelism modes and scales to thousands of GPUs. Stops short of embedded: the firm's own fund page keeps human researchers in the frame — 「策略研究员可以快速高效验证自己的想法，不受算力、模型大小等因素的制约」 (strategy researchers can validate their ideas quickly, unconstrained by compute or model size) — and no public source states that capital is committed without researchers setting and verifying the models or that the organisation was redesigned around AI, so METHODOLOGY §4 picks the lower stage. Confidence is med, not high: the adoption arc that justifies the stage runs 2016-2017, i.e. before the 2023 event floor, and rests on an undated own-domain page plus one T2 retrospective — no fetched 2023+ source describes a specific AI system operating inside the investment process itself.

name: KB Asset Management
rationale: KB자산운용 has AI in production on two fronts, both carried by enumerated Korean T2 reporting rather than by the firm's own voice — kbam.co.kr could not be read at all this session. 한국경제 (1 October 2025, 박주연 기자) states 「KB자산운용은 앤더슨을 기반으로 'KB 글로벌주식솔루션EMP 펀드', 'KB 올에셋AI솔루션EMP 펀드' 등을 운용 중이다」 — the firm currently runs two public EMP funds on 앤더슨(ANDERSON), the deep-learning portfolio system it 「독자적으로 구축」 (built independently) from 2016 — and the same paper's 19 September 2025 interview places that work in a named line organisation, 김홍곤 appearing as 「KB자산운용 AI퀀트&DI운용부문장」 (head of the AI Quant & DI investment division). A second, non-investment deployment followed: 서울경제 (6 March 2026, 장문항 기자) reports 「자산운용 업계 최초로 생성형 인공지능(AI) 기반의 아나운서를 자체 콘텐츠에 도입했다」 — a generative-AI announcer now producing the firm's ETF and fund explainers, market briefings, webinars and event video, claimed as an asset-management-industry first (company claim). Stops short of scaling: no admissible source quantifies the capital 앤더슨 actually runs, so the material-capital limb of the scaling bar cannot be tested; nothing in the public record shows AI used daily across the firm, the two EMP funds and the content tool being pockets rather than a firm-wide deployment; and no AI policy, governance body or use-case pipeline is disclosed anywhere — which under METHODOLOGY §4 means taking the lower of the two adjacent stages.

Arm-vs-parent: 'KB GenAI 포털', the agentic-AI environment 한국경제 (16 July 2025, 박재원 기자) says KB금융그룹 built in April 2025 as a financial-sector first, is the PARENT's platform, and the single sentence naming the asset manager is future-tense — 「국민은행, KB증권, …, KB자산운용, … 등 총 8개 계열사는 생성형 AI를 활용한 다양한 혁신금융서비스를 통해 맞춤형 금융 서비스를 제공할 계획이다」 — so §4 keeps it out of the stage. SEEN BUT NOT COUNTED, tier: the claim that KB자산운용's managers use 'KB-DAM' (the group investment-analysis platform built on 앤더슨) in fund management, and the widely repeated figure that AI-linked assets under management neared ₩1조 in June 2023, appear only in outlets below this project's bar (한국금융신문, 인공지능신문, 비즈워치, 대한경제, 머니S) — the ₩1조 figure is precisely what would test the material-capital clause, and it is why a human retry on those carriers, or on the firm's own domain, is the highest-value follow-up here. SOURCING: every fetch of kbam.co.kr failed TLS certificate verification, so no T1 own-domain source supports this row; 한국경제's 14 June 2023 article on the same AI-AUM figure returned HTTP 403 on both URL forms tried. AUM is the firm's total AUM as reported by 한국경제 on 21 May 2026 (이선아 기자) — 「KB자산운용의 총운용자산(AUM)이 200조원을 돌파했다」, crossed in April 2026.

name: Elo (Työeläkeyhtiö Elo)
rationale: Elo has AI running in named functions and a published AI-use policy, but nothing firm-wide. Its own Elomedia piece of 6 March 2024 reports a customer-service chatbot that handled 26,000 conversations during 2023 and resolved 77% of them without a human (60% positive user feedback), states that AI already supports the pension-granting decision process while a human always makes the decision itself, and names Microsoft M365 Copilot as an emerging tool. By June 2026 CEO Carl Pettersson described a further production use — AI analysis of population-level phenomena that weaken employees' work ability, including workload factors and patterns behind mental-health-related work disability, which client companies use to reduce disability risk — and, on the investment side, that "AI doesn't make investment decisions, but it supports investment operations, above all in the preparation of analyses" and in scenario modelling, alongside ICT renewal, background processes and customer service (company claims). The governance prong is met by Elo's own principles page, "Elon periaatteet tekoälyn käyttöön", which commits that "Elossa tekoälyä valvoo aina ihminen" (a human always supervises AI at Elo) and that Elo bears responsibility for why AI was used; the page carries no visible date, so under this project's sourcing rules it supports only that the policy exists. Stops short of scaling: no penetration, user-count or daily-use figure is public for any tool, the only dated deployment metrics are from 2023 and cover a single channel, no source describes firm-wide rollout or names AI as a strategic pillar, and Elo's own 14 August 2026 interim report makes no internal-AI claim at all.
footnote: Two scope calls. (i) The work-ability analytics are run by Elo on its own data and delivered to client companies as analysis; they are counted as internal operational use, not as METHODOLOGY §1(a) an AI product sold to clients — but the line is thin, and a reviewer who reads it as a client-facing service should drop that use case, which does not change the stage. (ii) Elo's investments in Finnish growth companies, including AI companies, are §1(b) AI as an investment thesis and are excluded. Separately, the Finance Finland trade-association write-up of 22 April 2026 corroborating the work-ability analytics is T3 and is therefore not cited as an event source.

name: KLP (Kommunal Landspensjonskasse)
rationale: KLP's entire public AI record is one interview. Speaking to IPE on 16 June 2026, EVP of technology Rune Hørnes says KLP is "in the early stages of adopting AI to improve efficiency across individual and organisational workflows" and is "gradually scaling in AI use across the organisation", and names the deployments: Microsoft Copilot with Edge and M365 for document drafting and structuring information, GitHub Copilot for software development, domain assistants described as BankingGPT and PropertyGPT, and Pythia — a KLP-developed AI assistant that "helps employees find and use internal knowledge across systems and domains". He reports "clear indications of improved individual productivity" and efficiency gains in software development (company claims), and places customer-facing use firmly at exploration: KLP is "just beginning to explore how AI can be used to improve our customer-facing services". Named internal tools in actual use, contained to productivity and development rather than the investment process, is what METHODOLOGY §3 calls piloting. Stops short of scaling: no user count, adoption rate or daily-use figure is disclosed for any tool, nothing places AI in the investment process, and the customer-facing work is explicitly not yet started. Confidence is low, not med, for a reason that is itself the finding: KLP's own disclosure does not corroborate a word of it. Its 2025 annual report contains no mention of kunstig intelligens, KI, AI, maskinlæring or Copilot anywhere, and its Q2 2026 report mentions artificial intelligence only as a driver of global economic activity. What that annual report does record is process automation — "KLP passerer en milepæl ved å ta i bruk helautomatisk behandling av alle nye søknader om alderspensjon" and a new digital pension system completed in 2025 that "automatiserer store deler av pensjonsbehandlingen" — which is rule-based automation of pension handling, not an AI claim, and is not counted toward the stage.
footnote: Read this row's evidence base before trusting the stage. (i) SINGLE-SOURCED: only one T1/T2 source describes KLP's internal AI at all — the IPE interview — where the project's bar is normally two events each with an independent T1/T2 source. This row was inserted at the reviewer's direction with the shortfall on the record rather than buried. (ii) The governance half of the piloting bar is NOT evidenced: Hørnes states governance as a requirement — "we need clear governance, guidelines, and user awareness" — not as something in place, and §4 reads a stated need as intent. A reviewer applying §4 strictly could hold this row at exploring on that alone; the case for piloting rests entirely on Pythia and GitHub Copilot being described as in use rather than planned. (iii) Two T3 sources corroborate the direction but cannot carry an event: Itera, a consultancy describing its own engagement (undated), says KLP had been "running pilot projects" whose "work lacked the most important strategic frameworks" and that it helped design a governance and operationalisation model; a Konsulentprisen write-up of 19 November 2025 on KLP's pension-platform programme cites "integrert bruk av KI-verktøy" and "KI-støtte for utvikling og regelverksforståelse" without naming a tool. (iv) Full automation of alderspensjon applications and the new digital pension system are process automation, not AI, and are excluded from the stage.
